text: Probably many of them were, at least partly. [[@body-temperature|Warm-blooded animals]], like birds and you, burn food to make their own body heat. Cold-blooded animals, like lizards and [[@croc-ancient|crocodiles]], mostly warm up by lying in the Sun.

For a long time, dinosaurs were pictured as giant, sluggish lizards. Today, the evidence points another way. Dinosaurs grew fast, many had [[@feathers|feathers]] for keeping warm, and some lived near the North Pole. The open question is how warm, and whether every kind of dinosaur was the same.

myth: Dinosaurs were slow, cold-blooded lizards that dragged their tails.

Footprints show their tails were held up, and bones show they grew fast. Many dinosaurs were active animals that made at least some of their own body heat, and their closest living relatives, birds, are fully warm-blooded.

sec.t:
When dinosaurs were first named in the 1840s, scientists thought of them as huge [[reptile|reptiles]]. Paintings showed them lumbering and dragging their tails in swamps. Then, in 1964, the American scientist John Ostrom found Deinonychus in Montana, a slim hunter with a big claw that looked built for leaping and slashing.

Ostrom argued it must have been active and agile, more like a bird than a lizard. His student Robert Bakker went further and said dinosaurs were fully warm-blooded. Their ideas started what is often called the "dinosaur [[@renaissance|renaissance]]", a rethink that changed how dinosaurs look in every museum.

Footprints helped too. Dinosaur trackways almost never show marks of a dragging tail. Tails were held up off the ground, balancing the body over the hips like a seesaw. Their legs stood straight under the body rather than sprawling out to the sides like a lizard's.

Some of the best evidence comes from [[@alaska|northern Alaska]]. Along the Colville River, scientists have found bones of many kinds of dinosaur, including babies that had only just hatched. Seventy million years ago this area was already far north. Winters had weeks of darkness and may have brought snow.

The world was warmer then, but these winters were still cold. A lizard-like animal could not have warmed up in the Sun for weeks on end. Raising young there suggests dinosaurs that could keep themselves warm from inside.

Not everyone thinks dinosaurs were as warm as birds. In 2014, one team compared growth rates of hundreds of living and [[extinct|extinct]] animals. They suggested many dinosaurs were "in-between", making some of their own heat without keeping it perfectly steady. Tuna, some sharks and leatherback turtles work a bit like this today.

Big animals also hold heat simply because of their size. A giant [[sauropod|sauropod]] lost heat slowly, the way a full pot of hot tea cools more slowly than a cup. It may have struggled more to keep cool than to keep warm. A small feathered hunter faced the opposite problem, which is one more reason the answer probably differed from one kind of dinosaur to another.

text: T. rex was bigger: about 12 m long and about as heavy as an elephant or more. Rajasaurus was about 8–9 m long and much lighter.

They never met. T. rex lived in North America and [[@rajasaurus|Rajasaurus]] in India, which was an island at the time. They weren't close cousins either. Big hunters [[evolve|evolved]] separately in different parts of the world.

sec.t:
Put the two next to each other and the difference is clear. T. rex was as long as a city bus, with a skull about 1.4 m long. Rajasaurus was as long as two cars parked end to end, with a shorter, deeper skull topped by a rounded crest.

Weight is where the gap is biggest. Studies of complete T. rex skeletons suggest adults weighed about 6 to 8 tonnes, more than an African elephant. Rajasaurus is known only from part of a skeleton, so nobody can weigh it with confidence. Its closest relatives were slimmer than tyrannosaurs, so it was probably a few tonnes at most.

For T. rex, scientists have several nearly complete skeletons, like Sue in Chicago. John Hutchinson's team made 3D [[@computers-how|computer models]] of them in 2011, adding flesh around the bones, and calculated their weight.

The heaviest T. rex estimate so far comes from a skeleton nicknamed Scotty, found in Saskatchewan, Canada, in 1991. In 2019, scientists suggested Scotty weighed nearly 9 tonnes, though other experts think that figure may be too high.

For Rajasaurus, only some bones were found: parts of the skull, backbone, hips and legs. Scientists compare these with close relatives like Majungasaurus, whose skeletons are more complete, and scale them up or down. It is careful [[@estimation|estimation]], and the answer comes with a range rather than a single number.

About 67 million years ago, India had broken away from Madagascar and was drifting north through the ocean, as you can read in [[@india-drift|India's long journey]]. North America was thousands of kilometres away, across oceans.

So the two lived at the same time, but in different worlds, a bit like [[@lions-gir|lions and tigers]] today. Wild lions live in Africa and in India's Gir forest, while tigers live only in Asia. India is the only country with both, and even there they live in different forests.

There is no way to stage a contest, and it would be a strange question to scientists. Each was suited to its own prey and land. T. rex had a bone-crushing bite. Abelisaurs like Rajasaurus had shorter, very strong skulls and may have held on to prey rather than tearing big chunks. Both were at the top of their [[foodchain|food chains]] until [[@extinction|the asteroid]] hit. After that, neither family left any [[descendant|descendants]], and the job of top hunter passed to others: giant ground birds and [[@croc-ancient|crocodiles]] in some places, and later mammals.

text: Weather satellites are cameras in space pointed at Earth. They take pictures of clouds, measure temperatures and sense water in the air, then beam the data to weather offices on the ground. Forecasters use the pictures to spot storms early and follow where they go.

There are two main kinds. Some sit very high up, about 35,800 kilometres above the [[equator|equator]], and watch the same half of the globe all the time. Others fly much lower, about 800 kilometres up, passing over the poles and scanning the whole planet in strips. Together they let forecasters see [[@cyclones-india|cyclones]] forming over empty ocean long before they reach land.

st.reveal: At about 35,800 km above the equator, a satellite takes exactly one day to go round Earth. Earth also spins once a day, so the satellite seems to hang still over one place, watching the same half of the planet all the time.

myth: Geostationary satellites sit still in space.
They are moving fast, at about 11,000 km per hour. They only seem to stay still because they go round Earth in exactly the time Earth takes to spin once.

sec.t:
A geostationary satellite circles Earth once a day, the same time Earth takes to spin. So it seems to hover over one place, like a lamp hanging over a table. It can photograph its half of the planet every few minutes, which makes it perfect for watching storms grow and move.

A polar-orbiting satellite is closer, so it sees finer detail. It sweeps from pole to pole while Earth turns beneath it, covering each place about twice a day. Its instruments can measure temperature and moisture at different heights in the air, which helps the computers that make [[@weather-forecasts|weather forecasts]].

Clouds are easy to photograph in daylight, but storms don't stop at night. So weather satellites also see in [[infrared|infrared]], a kind of light our eyes can't detect but which we feel as heat. Cold, high cloud tops show up clearly, and the coldest tops usually mean the strongest storms.

Another channel picks up water vapour, the invisible water in the air, showing rivers of moist air flowing across the oceans. Some low satellites use microwaves, which pass through cloud, to measure rain falling inside a storm or the speed of winds over the sea.

Satellites keep working after a storm has passed. Their pictures show flooded fields, swollen rivers and damaged forests, which helps rescue teams decide where to go first. Over months and years, the same measurements build a record of how sea temperatures, ice and clouds are changing.

{{story:cyclones-india}}

On 1 April 1960, the USA launched TIROS-1, the first successful weather satellite. Its first fuzzy television pictures showed cloud patterns over North America, and forecasters were thrilled. It worked for only 78 days, but it proved the idea.

Within a few years, satellites were spotting [[@hurricanes|hurricanes]] out in the Atlantic that ships and planes had missed. Today the USA's GOES satellites, Europe's Meteosat, Japan's Himawari and others share their pictures, so nearly the whole planet is watched all the time.

India's weather satellites watch the Indian Ocean, where the [[monsoon|monsoon]] and [[cyclone|cyclones]] are born. In 2002, ISRO launched its first satellite built only for weather. After the space shuttle Columbia disaster in 2003, it was renamed Kalpana-1 in honour of the astronaut [[@kalpana-chawla|Kalpana Chawla]].

Later came the INSAT-3D series. INSAT-3DS, launched in February 2024, sends images and readings to the India Meteorological Department. Like other [[@satellites-india|Indian satellites]], it is built and run by ISRO.

In October 1999, a super cyclone struck Odisha. Warnings did not reach enough people in time, and about 10,000 people died. Fourteen years later, in October 2013, Cyclone Phailin headed for the same coast with similar strength.

This time, satellites tracked Phailin for days as it grew over the Bay of Bengal. Forecasters predicted where and when it would land, and officials moved close to a million people to shelters. Phailin damaged many homes and crops, but the death toll was far lower. Forecasters still launch [[@weather-balloons|weather balloons]] and use radar, but the view from space now gives coastal towns days, not hours, to prepare.

text: Flying fish don't really fly like birds. They glide. When a [[predator|predator]] chases one, the fish swims fast towards the surface, up to about 60 km/h. It shoots out of the water and spreads its big, stiff pectoral fins, the fins just behind its head, like the wings of a [[@gliders|glider]].

Before leaving the water completely, it often beats the lower lobe of its tail against the surface very fast, like an outboard motor, to gain extra speed. Then it sails through the air for up to about 50 m, roughly half a football field, before splashing back down or touching the water to push off again.

It flaps its fins up and down like a bird

st.reveal: The fish races to the surface, spreads its fins and lifts its body out of the water. Only the lower part of its tail stays in, beating rapidly like an outboard motor until the fish lifts off and glides.

d.try: Make two paper planes from the same paper, one with wide, flat wings and one with narrow, pointed wings. Launch each gently from the same height, without throwing hard, and measure how far they glide. Wide, flat wings, like a flying fish's fins, usually glide further.
myth: Flying fish flap their fins like birds flap their wings.
Flying fish glide. They hold their fins out stiffly, like a paper plane. All their power comes from the tail, before and sometimes during the glide.

sec.t:
A flying fish's body is shaped like a torpedo, which helps it slice through water. Its pectoral fins are huge for a fish of its size, and some [[species|species]] also have large pelvic fins near the tail, giving them four "wings". These are called four-winged flying fish.

The lower part of the tail is longer than the upper part. That lets the fish keep its tail in the water while the rest of its body is in the air. Its eyes seem adapted to see well both underwater and in air, which is rare for a fish.

sec.h: Escape from below, danger from above

sec.t:
Most glides last a few seconds and stay within a metre or two of the waves, though gusts can lift a fish several metres up. By touching the water with its tail and beating again, a flying fish can stay up much longer, skipping like a stone across a pond. In 2008, a Japanese TV crew on a ferry near the island of Yakushima filmed one gliding for 45 seconds, the longest recorded flight.

Scientists have tested flying fish in wind tunnels and found they glide about as efficiently as some birds, such as hawks. Their fins hold out flat and stiff, which gives them steady lift, much like a well-made paper plane.

About 70 kinds of flying fish live in warm oceans around the world, including the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal. Fishermen in India catch them too. In Barbados, flying fish are so loved that the island is called the land of the flying fish. The national dish is cou-cou and flying fish, and the fish appears on its coins.

In Japan, flying fish eggs are tiny, crunchy, orange beads called tobiko, often sprinkled on [[@sushi|sushi]]. Flying fish lay sticky eggs on floating seaweed and other drifting things, and fishers in some places catch them by floating bundles of leaves for the fish to lay on.

Flying fish are not the only animals that glide. Flying squirrels, flying lizards and even flying snakes in South and South-East Asia leap from trees and sail through the air. None of them can climb higher by flapping. Only [[@how-birds-fly|birds]], bats and insects can stay up by flapping. And baby spiders have an odder trick still: they let out silk threads and drift on the wind for kilometres, one of many ways to [[@fly-without-wings|fly without wings]].

text: The Titanic sank because it hit an [[@why-ice-floats|iceberg]] at night, at high speed, in the North Atlantic Ocean. The collision opened gaps along the right-hand side of the hull below the waterline. Seawater poured into the front of the ship. The Titanic was built to stay afloat with up to four of its front compartments flooded, but at least five began filling. The bow sank lower, water spilled over the walls into the next compartments, and the ship was doomed.

It struck the iceberg at about 11:40 pm on 14 April 1912 and sank at about 2:20 am on 15 April. Of about 2,200 people on board, around 1,500 died, many in the freezing water. There were not enough lifeboats for everyone.

st.prompt: The Titanic had about 2,200 people on board. Its lifeboats had room for about how many?

options.t: All of them, with spare seats

st.reveal: The 20 lifeboats could hold about 1,178 people, a little over half. The safety rules of 1912 were based on a ship's weight, not on how many passengers it carried. And many boats were lowered only partly full.

A few magazines and newspapers called ships like it "practically unsinkable", but its owners did not make it a big promise. The idea that everyone believed it grew much stronger after the disaster, in books and films.

sec.t:
The Titanic was the largest moving object people had ever built. It was about 269 m long, nearly as long as three football fields, and as tall as a 17-storey building from keel to the tops of its funnels. It had a gym, a swimming pool, restaurants and grand staircases for its richest passengers. Most people on board, though, travelled in second and third class, including many [[@immigration-stories|families moving to America]] for a new life.

Its first voyage left Southampton in England on 10 April 1912, bound for [[@new-york|New York]]. Steel ships like it float because their hulls push aside a huge weight of water, as you can read in [[@floating-ships|how ships float]].

The Titanic's wireless operators sent distress calls, including the new SOS signal, using [[@radio-invented|radio]], which was still a young invention. A nearby ship, the Californian, was probably close enough to help, but its radio operator had gone to bed and switched off his set.

The Carpathia, about 100 km away, heard the call and raced through the ice. It arrived about an hour and a half after the Titanic sank and rescued about 700 survivors from the lifeboats. Many lifeboats had left half empty, partly because at first many passengers did not believe the ship could sink.

The disaster shocked the world and changed the rules of the sea. In 1914, nations signed the first international agreement on safety at sea. Ships now had to carry enough lifeboats for everyone on board, hold lifeboat drills and keep their radios on day and night. An International Ice Patrol was set up to watch for icebergs in the North Atlantic. It still operates today.

The wreck lay hidden for 73 years. In 1985, a team led by Robert Ballard of the USA and Jean-Louis Michel of France found it about 3,800 m down, broken in two. Remote cameras and deep-diving vehicles have visited it since, as you can read in [[@ocean-explorers|ocean explorers]]. Tiny living things are slowly eating away its iron, and one day little of it may be left.

text: Goats and sheep were among the first animals ever kept on farms, about 10,000–11,000 years ago in West Asia. People kept them because they were so practical. They could live on rough grass and shrubs that people couldn't eat, and turn them into milk, meat, skins and later wool. They were small enough to handle, lived in herds that followed a leader, and had young quickly.
For early farmers, a flock was like a walking store cupboard. Instead of hunting wild animals that might run away, families could keep food alive and close by, all year round.

sec.t:
Wild goats called bezoar ibex lived in the Zagros Mountains, along today's border of Iran and Iraq. At a site called Ganj Dareh, [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] found goat bones about 10,000 years old. The bones showed that people were killing mostly young males and keeping females to breed, a sign of herding, not hunting.

Sheep came from a wild sheep called the Asiatic mouflon, found in the hills of today's Turkey, Iraq and Iran. In South Asia, at Mehrgarh in Balochistan, people were keeping goats and sheep by about 7000 BCE, alongside early wheat and barley [[@farming-began|farming]].

Goats are browsers. Instead of just grazing on grass like sheep, they nibble leaves, twigs and bushes, often standing on their back legs to reach. In Morocco, goats even climb argan trees to eat the fruit. They can survive in dry, rocky places where cows would starve.

Their eyes are built for watching out. The rectangular pupils give a very wide view, so a goat can see [[predator|predators]] coming while its head is down. Goats are also curious and quick to learn, and studies have shown they can remember how to solve a food puzzle for months.

India has huge flocks. The 2019 livestock [[census|census]] counted about 14.9 crore goats and 7.4 crore sheep. For many families with little land, goats are a kind of savings account: they breed quickly and can be sold when money is needed. Mahatma Gandhi famously drank goat's milk for much of his life.

In the high, cold desert of [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], Changthangi goats survive winters of minus 30 °C or colder. Their fine, soft undercoat is combed out each spring to make pashmina, one of the most prized wools in the world. Sheep herders like the Gaddis of Himachal Pradesh and the Rabaris of Gujarat and Rajasthan still walk their flocks between summer and winter pastures, as their ancestors did for centuries.

In 1996, scientists in Scotland created Dolly, the first [[mammal|mammal]] cloned from an adult cell. She was a sheep, and she became one of the most famous animals in science. She was named after the singer Dolly Parton, and she had six lambs of her own. Today, sheep and goats live almost everywhere people do, from Welsh hillsides and the ranches of the American West to village lanes in Rajasthan.

text: Most glass begins as ordinary-looking [[@sand-where|sand]] made of silica, also called silicon dioxide. Glassmakers mix it with soda ash, which lowers the melting point, and limestone, which makes the glass tough and stops it [[dissolve|dissolving]] in water. Often they add broken recycled glass too, which melts more easily.
The mixture goes into a huge furnace and is heated to about 1,500°C or more, until it becomes a glowing, syrupy liquid. Then it is shaped, by blowing, pressing, pouring or floating, and cooled.

In sand, the [[atom|atoms]] are lined up in neat repeating patterns called crystals. When melted glass cools fairly quickly, its atoms freeze in place in a jumble before they can line up. That jumble is what makes glass clear, smooth and hard.

sec.t:
The first glass objects were small beads, made in [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]] about 4,500 years ago. For a long time, glass was rare and precious, worn as jewellery or used for small bottles.

About 2,000 years ago, craftspeople around the eastern Mediterranean discovered glassblowing. A glassblower gathers a blob of molten glass on the end of a long metal pipe, then blows into it, like blowing up a balloon. With turning, swinging and shaping tools, the blob becomes a bottle, a bowl or a vase. Glassblowing made glass cheaper and spread it across the Roman Empire.

Glass beads were also made in ancient India, and [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] have found them at sites from more than 2,000 years ago, including in the south.

Making large, flat, perfectly clear window glass was hard for centuries. Panes were blown and spun into discs, or rolled and polished, which took time and money.

In the 1950s, the British engineer Alastair Pilkington had a better idea. His team poured molten glass onto a bath of melted tin. The glass floated on top like oil on water and spread into a perfectly flat, smooth sheet. This float glass process was introduced in 1959. Almost all window glass in the world is made this way today, from homes to the tall glass towers of Mumbai and New York.

In Uttar Pradesh, the city of Firozabad has been a centre of glassmaking for generations. It is famous for colourful glass bangles, which are worn across India, especially at weddings and festivals. Many families work in small workshops, shaping, joining and decorating bangles by hand after they come from the furnaces.

Glass can be coloured by adding small amounts of metals. Cobalt makes deep blue, chromium makes green, and gold can make a rich ruby red. The great stained-glass windows of [[@gothic-cathedrals|Gothic cathedrals]] in Europe got their glowing colours this way. Unlike paper or plastic, glass can be [[@recycling|recycled]] again and again without losing quality.

text: Bhangra is a lively folk dance and music from [[@punjab|Punjab]], the region shared by north-west [[@pakistan-history|India and Pakistan]]. It is driven by the deep, bouncing beat of the dhol, a big double-sided drum. Dancers raise their arms high, bounce their shoulders, hop, kick and spin, often shouting "balle balle" or "hoi" in time with the music.

It began as a celebration of the harvest, especially at Baisakhi in April, when the wheat crop is gathered. Today bhangra is danced at weddings, festivals, college competitions and parties, and it has become one of South Asia's best-known dances worldwide. Its music has blended with pop, [[@reggae|reggae]] and [[@hip-hop|hip-hop]] to make a sound that is played in clubs from London to Los Angeles.

sec.t:
For centuries, farmers in Punjab worked hard through the winter to grow wheat. When the golden crop was ready in spring, villages celebrated. Men danced in a circle around a dhol player, while someone sang short, funny or proud verses called *boliyan* about village life, love and farming.

Many steps copy farm work, such as sowing seeds or swinging a sickle. Women had their own dance, giddha, with clapping, teasing songs and graceful movements. Today women and girls dance bhangra too, and many teams are mixed.

In 1947, Punjab was divided between India and Pakistan during [[@partition|Partition]]. Millions of people were forced from their homes. In the years that followed, Punjabis on both sides kept their music and dance alive as a way of holding on to their culture.

In Indian Punjab, colleges and dance teams developed a new, stage-ready bhangra in the 1950s and 1960s. They combined steps from several regional dances, such as jhummar and luddi. They also added bright matching costumes: a kurta, a wrapped cloth called a tehmat, a waistcoat and a turban with a fan-shaped turla on top. This is the style most people now think of as bhangra.

Punjabis who moved to Britain in the 1960s and 1970s took their music with them. In the 1980s, bands in Birmingham and Southall mixed traditional bhangra songs with drum machines, synthesisers and electric guitars. Young British Asians danced to it at daytime parties, and a new sound was born.

In 1998, Panjabi MC released "Mundian To Bach Ke", which mixed bhangra with a TV theme tune. It became a huge hit across Europe a few years later, and an American rapper made a remix. That same year in India, Daler Mehndi's "Tunak Tunak Tun" became famous across the country and, later, on the internet.

Today, university bhangra teams in the United States, Canada and Britain compete in big inter-college competitions. At Indian weddings, almost every family has someone who will start a bhangra the moment the dhol begins. The beat that once marked the end of a farming year now marks celebrations of every kind.

text: India's great temple [[sculpture|sculptures]] were carved by hand. Teams of sculptors used iron chisels and hammers to cut away stone, bit by bit, until gods, dancers, elephants and flowers appeared.

They did not work alone or make it up as they went. A master builder, the sthapati, planned the temple. Old texts called the Shilpa Shastras set out rules for how each god should stand, what it should hold and how its body should be measured.

Some sculptures were carved separately and set into the walls. Others were cut straight out of the living rock, still joined to a cliff or boulder. The result is thousands of temples covered with figures, from Konark in the east to the Hoysala temples of Karnataka.

options.t: A soft stone that hardens after it is quarried
Very hard granite polished with diamonds

st.reveal: They used a soapstone-like rock, a kind of schist. It is soft enough to carve finely when freshly cut and grows harder as it is exposed to the air, which helped the fine details survive about 800 years.

myth: Ancient temple sculptures were made by pouring stone into moulds.

The stone figures were cut by hand from solid rock with iron chisels and hammers. You can still see chisel marks on unfinished carvings at sites like Mamallapuram, where some panels were left half done.

sec.t:
How do many carvers make figures that match? The texts gave them a measuring system. One common unit was the length of the figure's own face, from hairline to chin, called a tala.

A standing god might be nine or ten face-lengths tall. Arms, eyes and fingers each had a set size. This let a group of carvers work on different parts of a temple and still keep everything in proportion, the way a recipe lets cooks in different kitchens make the same dish. It also gave the figures their balance and [[@symmetry|symmetry]].

At [[@india-wonder-shore-temple|Mamallapuram]], south of Chennai, sculptors of the [[@pallavas|Pallava]] kings worked in the 7th century. Their most famous work, often called Arjuna's Penance or the Descent of the Ganga, covers two huge boulders about 29 m long. More than a hundred figures crowd onto it: gods, people, a cat standing on its hind legs and life-size elephants.

A crack runs down the middle. The carvers made it into a river, with snake beings swimming up it.

At Ellora in Maharashtra, in the 8th century, the Kailasa temple was cut from a single hill of [[basalt|basalt]]. Workers dug trenches around a block of rock, then carved the temple inside it from the top down. There was no room for big mistakes, since nothing could be glued back on. How they planned [[@ellora-kailasa|the Kailasa temple]] so precisely is something [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] still argue about.

{{story:rocks-types}}

The [[@hoysalas|Hoysala]] kings of Karnataka built temples at Belur and Halebidu in the 12th and 13th centuries. Their sculptors used a soapstone-like rock, a kind of schist. It is soft when freshly cut, so carvers could make bead necklaces, curling hair and bangles that stand away from the body.

Some Hoysala sculptors signed their work. Names such as Mallitamma appear on carvings, so for once we know who made them.

Carvers started by splitting stone with wedges, then roughed out the shape with heavy chisels. Finer chisels came next, then files and polishing with sand or other stones. A single panel could take months, and a large temple could take several generations to finish.

Stone was not the only material. The bronze gods carried out in temple processions were made a different way, by casting. In Swamimalai, in Tamil Nadu, artists still model each figure in wax, cover it in clay and pour in molten metal, an ancient method you can learn about in [[@bronze-casting|bronze casting]].

The craft passed down in families from parent to child. It hasn't died out. Mamallapuram still has a government college of sculpture, and its streets are lined with workshops where you can hear the tap of hammers. Temples being built today in India and abroad, including in the USA, often hire these carvers, who still check the old proportions before they start.

text: India's Parliament has two houses. The Lok Sabha, or House of the People, is directly elected by voters. The Rajya Sabha, or Council of States, represents India's states and union [[territory|territories]], and most of its members are elected by state legislators.

Both must pass a bill for it to become law. But the Lok Sabha is more powerful. The government needs its support to stay in office, and on money matters it has the final word. The Rajya Sabha is often described as the house of second thoughts. It checks, questions and sometimes slows down what the Lok Sabha passes. Both houses first met in May 1952.

st.prompt: Which house can vote a government out of power with a no-confidence motion?
st.reveal: The government must keep the support of a majority in the Lok Sabha, because its members are directly elected. A no-confidence motion can only be moved there. The Rajya Sabha can question and criticise the government, but cannot remove it.

sec.t:
The Rajya Sabha has up to 250 members. At present 233 are elected by the members of state and union territory assemblies, and 12 are nominated by the President for their work in art, literature, science or social service. The singer [[@lata-mangeshkar|Lata Mangeshkar]] and the cricketer [[@sachin-tendulkar|Sachin Tendulkar]] have both been nominated members.

Members must be at least 30 and serve six-year terms. The house is never dissolved. Instead, a third of its members retire every two years and are replaced, so it changes gradually. The Vice-President of India chairs it.

For most bills, both houses must agree. If they disagree, the President can call a joint sitting, where members of both houses vote together. Since the Lok Sabha is more than twice as big, it usually wins. This has happened only three times: in 1961, 1978 and 2002.

Money bills, such as those about taxes, work differently. They can only start in the Lok Sabha. The Rajya Sabha can suggest changes within 14 days, but the Lok Sabha can ignore them.

The Rajya Sabha has its own special powers. With a two-thirds vote, it can allow Parliament to make laws on a subject normally left to [[@states-india|the states]], if it is in the national interest.

Many [[democracy|democracies]] have two houses. America's [[@congress-usa|Congress]] has a House of Representatives, elected by population, and a Senate, with two senators from every state. Britain has the elected House of Commons and the House of Lords, whose members are appointed or [[inherit|inherit]] their seats.

India's system borrows from both. Like the US Senate, the Rajya Sabha speaks for the states, though bigger states send more members. Like Britain's Commons, the Lok Sabha decides who governs. Having two houses means laws get a second look before they reach everyone in the country.

text: UN peacekeepers are soldiers, police and civilian experts sent by the United Nations to help countries move from war towards peace. They might watch over a ceasefire line, protect villagers, help [[refugee|refugees]] return home, clear landmines, train police or help run elections.

The UN has no army of its own. Countries lend their troops and police for each mission, and they wear blue helmets or berets, which is why they are often called the "Blue Helmets". Peacekeepers are supposed to be neutral. They usually go only where the main sides in a conflict have agreed to let them in.

st.prompt: When are UN peacekeepers allowed to use force?

options.t: Mostly in self-defence and to protect their mission and civilians
Whenever they choose a side to help win
Never, they carry no weapons at all

st.reveal: Peacekeeping rests on three principles. The main parties must agree to the mission, peacekeepers stay impartial, and they use force only in self-defence or to defend their mandate, which often includes protecting civilians.

The UN has no army of its own. Peacekeepers are soldiers and police lent by member countries for each mission, and they wear their own country's uniform with a UN blue helmet or beret.

sec.t:
India has been one of the biggest contributors of peacekeepers in UN history. More than 2.5 lakh Indian soldiers and police have served since the 1950s, in places from [[@seoul|Korea]] and the Congo to Lebanon, South Sudan and Cambodia. More than 150 Indians have died while serving. In the Congo in 1961, Captain Gurbachan Singh Salaria was killed leading a charge against armed fighters. He was awarded the Param Vir Chakra, India's highest military honour, the only time it has been given for a UN mission.

In 2007, India sent the first all-women formed police unit to a UN mission, in Liberia, which was recovering from a long civil war. The officers patrolled streets, guarded government buildings and ran night patrols. Liberian women reportedly joined the country's police in larger numbers after seeing them at work. The unit served until 2016.

Peacekeeping is dangerous. Missions often work in places where fighting hasn't fully stopped, with armed groups that don't respect the rules. Since 1948, more than 4,000 peacekeepers from many countries have died in service.

There have also been painful failures. In Rwanda in 1994 and at Srebrenica in Bosnia in 1995, small UN forces were unable to stop terrible mass killings. Peacekeepers in Haiti were linked to a [[@disease-history|cholera]] outbreak in 2010, and the UN later apologised. There have also been cases of peacekeepers abusing the people they were meant to protect. The UN has introduced stricter rules, though critics say more needs to be done.

All UN member countries share the cost, with richer countries paying more. The USA is the largest single funder. Most troops, though, come from countries in South Asia and Africa, including India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Rwanda and Ethiopia.

Today most missions are in Africa and the Middle East. They often last many years. The mission in Cyprus, for example, began in 1964 and still patrols a buffer zone across the island. Many peacekeepers say the job is worth it when a market reopens or children go back to school. The work is tied closely to [[@human-rights|human rights]], because a ceasefire matters most when ordinary people can live safely again.

text: A refugee is someone who has had to flee their own country because they are in danger there, from war, violence or [[persecution|persecution]]. Persecution means being hunted, jailed or hurt because of your religion, ethnic group, politics or who you are.

Refugees are different from migrants who choose to move for work or study. A refugee leaves because staying could cost them their life or freedom. People who flee but stay inside their own country are called internally displaced.

The [[@united-nations|United Nations]] says more than 10 crore (100 million) people around the world have been forced from their homes. A world [[treaty|treaty]] from 1951 protects refugees, and a UN agency called UNHCR helps them.

st.reveal: Einstein was Jewish and lived in Germany. When the Nazis came to power in 1933, he was abroad and decided not to return. He settled in the United States, where he lived for the rest of his life.

sec.t:
After the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], millions of people across Europe had no home to go back to. In 1950, the United Nations set up its refugee agency, UNHCR. The next year, countries agreed the Refugee Convention.

Its most important rule is that a refugee must not be sent back to a country where they face serious danger. Countries that joined it, including the USA, promise to give refugees fair treatment, such as the right to go to court and send children to school. The USA joined in 1968, through a 1967 update to the treaty. UNHCR has won the [[@nobel-peace|Nobel Peace Prize]] twice for its work.

sec.h: India's long history of sheltering people

sec.t:
Some of the world's best-known people were once refugees. [[@einstein|Albert Einstein]] left Germany when the [[@holocaust|Nazis]] came to power in 1933. The writer [[@anne-frank|Anne Frank]]'s family fled Germany for the Netherlands. The former US Secretary of State Madeleine Albright arrived in America as a child refugee from Czechoslovakia.

These names are famous. Most refugees are not, but they too bring skills, food, languages and stories to the places that take them in.

Some refugees live in camps for years, in tents or simple shelters, waiting for peace. Others rent rooms in cities and look for work. Children may miss years of school, which is why aid groups set up classrooms in camps.

In the end, refugees usually hope for one of three things: to go home safely, to settle in the country where they first sheltered, or to be welcomed in a third country. The USA has resettled millions of refugees since 1980, when it passed a law setting out how.

A person who arrives in a new country and asks to be protected as a refugee is called an asylum seeker. Officials then check their story, which can take months or even years. If they are accepted, they are given refugee status and allowed to stay.

Countries argue a lot about how many people to accept and how fast to decide. Those debates are often in the news. The 1951 Convention sets the basic rules, but each country runs its own system.

In 2016, ten refugee athletes competed at the Rio Olympics under the Olympic flag. The Refugee Olympic Team has returned at every Games since. Every year on 20 June, World Refugee Day honours the courage of people who had to start again somewhere new.

text: A smart city uses [[sensor|sensors]], internet connections and computers to run everyday services better. Traffic lights can change their timing when a road is busy. Water pipes can report a leak. Buses can send their location to an app, so you know when the next one is coming.

The idea is that data, collected all the time and from all over the city, helps officials spot problems early and fix them faster. A smart city should also be easier for people to live in, with cleaner streets, safer roads and less waiting.

There is no exact rule for what counts as "smart". Different cities use the word in quite different ways. For some it means free Wi-Fi in the park. For others it means a whole new city wired from the ground up.

st.reveal: Most of the money went into upgrading chosen areas of existing cities, such as a market district or a stretch of riverfront. Each city also built a control centre to watch traffic, water and other services in one place.

A few, like Songdo in South Korea, were built on empty land. Most smart city projects, in India and elsewhere, add sensors, apps and better services to cities people already live in.

sec.t:
Much of a smart city is an example of the [[@internet-of-things|internet of things]]: ordinary objects fitted with small sensors that send information over the internet. A dustbin might report when it is full, so the collection truck only stops where it is needed. Streetlights might dim when nobody is around, saving power.

Cameras at junctions can count cars, and [[@traffic-lights|traffic lights]] can use those counts to decide how long to stay green. Electricity meters can report usage every few minutes instead of once a month.

All of this data flows into a control room, where staff watch maps and alerts on big screens, a bit like [[@air-traffic|air traffic controllers]] for a whole city.

{{story:internet-of-things}}

In June 2015, the Government of India launched the Smart Cities Mission. Cities competed to join, and 100 were chosen in rounds between 2016 and 2018. Bhubaneswar came first in the first list.

Each city chose an area to upgrade, such as an old market, a lakefront or a station area, and added projects like smart roads, [[@renewable-energy|solar panels]] and better drainage. Every city also set up an Integrated Command and Control Centre. During the COVID-19 [[pandemic|pandemic]] in 2020, several cities used these rooms to track cases and organise supplies.

The mission's deadline was pushed back more than once, finally to March 2025.

A few places really were built new. Songdo, near [[@seoul|Seoul]] in South Korea, was built on land reclaimed from the sea, with sensors and pipes planned in from the start. Its rubbish is sucked away through underground tubes instead of being collected by trucks.

[[@singapore|Singapore]] took a different route. In 2014 it launched a plan it called Smart Nation, adding sensors, digital services and data across a city that already existed. In the USA, cities such as New York have put sensors on streets and buildings to study noise, air and traffic.

Smart cities raise real worries. A city full of cameras and sensors knows a great deal about where people go. Some cities use [[@face-recognition|face recognition]] on their cameras, which many people see as a threat to [[@privacy|privacy]]. Who owns the data, and who can see it?

Another question is who benefits. Critics of India's mission point out that many projects improved only a small area, while poorer neighbourhoods saw little change. Supporters reply that the mission gave cities their first real tools for managing traffic, water and emergencies. Both sides agree on one thing: technology helps only if the basic pipes, drains and buses work too.

text: An exponent, or power, is a short way to write repeated multiplication. Instead of writing 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2, you write 2⁵. The big number, 2, is called the base. The small raised number, 5, is the exponent. It tells you how many 2s to multiply together. 2⁵ is 32.

Powers grow very fast, which is why they are useful for describing huge and tiny numbers. Scientists use them to write the distance to stars, the size of [[atom|atoms]] and the number of cells in your body without filling a page with zeros.

st.prompt: You start with 1 grain of rice on the first square of a chessboard and double it on each square. Roughly how many grains are on the 11th square?
st.reveal: The 11th square has 2¹⁰ grains, which is 1,024. By the 21st square it passes a million, and by the 64th it is more than 9 quintillion. Doubling starts slowly, then explodes.

d.try: Take a sheet of newspaper and fold it in half as many times as you can. Count the layers after each fold: 2, 4, 8, 16. Most people can't get past 7 or 8 folds, because by then the stack is over a hundred layers thick. Write the number of layers as a power of 2.
myth: 2³ means 2 × 3, which is 6.
2³ means 2 multiplied by itself three times, 2 × 2 × 2, which is 8. The exponent counts how many times the number appears in the multiplication.

sec.t:
You already know two powers. 5² is read "five squared", and it equals 25, [[@area-volume|the area of a square]] with sides of 5. 5³ is "five cubed", and equals 125, the number of small cubes in a big cube 5 on each side. That is where the names come from.

There are a couple of odd rules. Any number to the power 1 is just itself. And any number, except 0, to the power 0 is 1. That sounds strange, but it follows a pattern: 2³ is 8, 2² is 4, 2¹ is 2, and each step halves the answer. Halve once more and you get 2⁰ = 1.

Paper folding shows the same explosion. A sheet of paper is about 0.1 mm thick. Fold it once and it is 2 layers thick. Fold it 10 times and it would be 2¹⁰, or 1,024, layers: about 10 cm. Fold it 42 times and it would be 2⁴² layers, more than 400,000 km, past the Moon, which is about 384,000 km away.

In real life you can't [[@puzzle-folding-paper-moon|fold paper that many times]], because each fold needs far more paper than the last. In 2002, an American student named Britney Gallivan set a record of 12 folds, using a very long strip of paper. In 2011, students at a school in Massachusetts managed 13 folds with a strip of toilet paper about 16 km long.

Powers of 10 are especially handy. 10² is 100, 10³ is 1,000, and 10⁶ is a million. The exponent tells you how many zeros follow the 1. In India, 1 lakh is 10⁵ and 1 crore is 10⁷.

Scientists write big numbers as a small number times a power of 10. The Sun is about 1.5 × 10⁸ km away, or [[@space-distances|150 million km]]. A [[@light-years|light-year]] is about 9.5 × 10¹² km. For tiny things, they use negative powers: a typical bacterium is about 10⁻⁶ m, a millionth of a metre, across.

Exponents also describe things that double, like [[bacteria|bacteria]] splitting in a warm lunchbox or money growing with [[@maths-money-compound|compound interest]]. Something that doubles every 20 minutes can go from one cell to over a million in less than seven hours, because 2²⁰ is more than a million.

text: A paradox is an argument that starts from ideas that seem obviously true and arrives at something that seems obviously false or impossible. It feels like a trick, and sometimes it is. Other times, the strange answer turns out to be correct and it's our instinct that was wrong.

Paradoxes come in a few kinds. Some are puzzles about words and [[@logic|logic]]. Some are about [[@infinity|infinity]]. Some are about chance, where the true answer just feels wrong. Mathematicians love them because each one exposes a weak spot in how we think.

st.prompt: A game show has three doors. A car is behind one, goats behind the others. You pick a door. The host, who knows where the car is, opens another door to show a goat. Should you switch?

options.t: Yes, switching wins two times out of three

st.reveal: Your first pick had a 1-in-3 chance. The host's door was not random, because he always shows a goat, so the other closed door carries the leftover 2-in-3 chance. Playing it many times with cups and a coin proves it.

sec.t:
Around 450 BCE, the Greek thinker Zeno of Elea told a story. Achilles, the fastest runner, races a tortoise that has a head start. By the time Achilles reaches where the tortoise was, it has crept a little further. By the time he reaches that point, it has moved again. This goes on forever, so how can he ever pass it?

Of course runners do overtake. The answer came much later, with the maths of limits. An endless list of ever-smaller steps can add up to a finite distance. Half a metre, plus a quarter, plus an eighth, and so on, never goes past one metre.

Infinity causes other headaches. The German mathematician David Hilbert described a hotel with endless rooms, every one of them full. A new guest arrives. No problem: everyone moves from room n to room n + 1, and room 1 is free. Endless sets simply don't behave like ordinary ones.

sec.h: Sentences that bite their own tail
When the right answer feels wrong
sec.t:
Some paradoxes have perfectly clear answers. They just clash with our gut feeling. Take birthdays. With 23 people in a room, the chance that at least two [[@puzzle-birthday|share a birthday]] is just over 50%. With 70 people, it's above 99.9%.

It seems too high because we think about our own birthday. But the question is about any pair, and 23 people make 253 different pairs. That's a lot of chances for a match.

The [[@puzzle-monty-hall|Monty Hall puzzle]] is another. When the columnist Marilyn vos Savant explained in 1990 that switching doors wins two times in three, she was flooded with letters calling her wrong. Computer simulations and simple experiments with cups proved her right.

Paradoxes also turn up outside maths. In the old Ship of Theseus puzzle, a ship's planks are replaced one by one until none of the original wood is left. Is it the same ship? Science fiction loves the grandfather paradox: what happens if a time traveller stops their own grandparents from meeting?

Physics has real puzzles too. In [[@einstein|Einstein]]'s theory, a twin who flies fast through space comes back younger than the twin who stayed at home. It sounds like a paradox, but experiments with very precise clocks on fast planes and [[@time-in-space|satellites]] show that time really does stretch. Sometimes the universe is simply stranger than common sense.

text: "Indie" is short for independent. In India it usually means music made outside the film industry and the big record companies. That covers rock bands in Shillong and Bengaluru, rappers in Mumbai's lanes, singer-songwriters with one guitar, and folk musicians mixing old songs with electronic beats.

For decades, almost all popular music in India came from films, so indie musicians struggled to be heard. Cheap recording, [[@youtube|YouTube]] and streaming apps changed that. Today an artist can record a song in a bedroom, upload it, and find listeners in Kolkata and California on the same day.

sec.h: Life in the shadow of films
sec.t:
[[@bollywood-music|Bollywood songs]] and other film music have been India's most popular music since the 1930s. Radio, cassettes and TV mostly played [[@film-songs|film songs]], so record companies had little reason to sign anyone else.

In the 1990s, music TV channels like MTV and Channel V arrived. A short "Indipop" boom followed, with singers such as Lucky Ali and groups such as Colonial Cousins and Euphoria. Their songs had videos, not films, behind them. The boom faded by the 2000s, but it showed that young listeners wanted something different.

Rock bands had been playing in India long before. Indian Ocean, formed in Delhi in 1990, mixed rock with folk and classical sounds. Parikrama in Delhi and Thermal and a Quarter in Bengaluru built fans by playing at college festivals, which were among the few places a band could perform to thousands.

In Kerala, the band Avial sang rock in Malayalam, borrowing tunes and [[rhythm|rhythms]] from old [[@folk-music-india|folk songs]]. Many bands sang in English at first, but more and more now choose Hindi, Tamil, Bengali or other languages. Singing in your own language, many musicians say, lets them write about the streets and people they actually know.

From 2010, the NH7 Weekender festival in Pune brought indie bands to big outdoor crowds. In 2012, the Ziro Festival of Music began in a valley of rice fields in Arunachal Pradesh. Musicians play on stages made of bamboo, and campers sleep in tents among the paddy.

These festivals gave indie artists something they had lacked: a place to meet fans face to face. They also helped bands earn money from tickets, T-shirts and sponsors, since few indie songs ever made much from record sales. A band that played well at one festival might be invited to a dozen more that year.

In the 2010s, young rappers in Mumbai began writing about life in their neighbourhoods, in Hindi and local slang. This style of [[@hip-hop|hip-hop]] was called gully rap, from the word for a narrow lane. The 2019 film Gully Boy was inspired by real Mumbai rappers.

Singer-songwriters found audiences online too. Prateek Kuhad's love song "cold/mess" spread far enough that Barack Obama named it one of his favourite songs of 2019. It is a long way from the days when a song needed a film to be heard.

text: Satyajit Ray was a film director, writer and artist from Kolkata. His first film, *Pather Panchali* (1955), told the story of a poor village family through the eyes of a small boy named Apu. It won a prize at the [[@film-festivals|Cannes Film Festival]] in 1956 and made many people around the world take notice of Indian films.

Ray went on to make about 30 feature films, many of them in Bengali. He wrote the scripts, drew the posters and, later, composed the music himself. Children in Bengal also know him as the author of the [[@satyajit-ray-stories|Feluda]] [[@detective-stories|detective stories]].

st.reveal: Ray had spent his savings and pawned his wife's jewellery, but filming still stopped for months. The Government of West Bengal finally paid for the rest, which is how one of the world's most admired films came to be owned by a state government.

sec.t:
Ray grew up surrounded by books and pictures. His grandfather, Upendrakishore Ray Chowdhury, started a [[@childrens-magazines|children's magazine]] called *Sandesh* in 1913. His father, [[@sukumar-ray|Sukumar Ray]], wrote funny nonsense poems that Bengali children still recite. Sukumar died when Satyajit was only two.

As a young man, Satyajit studied art at Santiniketan, the university founded by [[@tagore|Rabindranath Tagore]]. Then he worked in an advertising company in Calcutta, designing book covers. One of the books he illustrated was a children's version of *Pather Panchali*. He began to picture it as a film.

*Pather Panchali* became the first part of the Apu Trilogy, followed by *Aparajito* (1956) and *Apur Sansar* (1959). The trilogy follows Apu from childhood to adulthood. Many film schools still use it to teach how to tell a story with pictures.

In 1961 Ray revived his grandfather's *Sandesh* magazine. To fill its pages, he invented Feluda, a sharp-eyed detective from [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], and Professor Shonku, a scientist whose inventions take him across the world. He also made two Feluda films. For more Indian comics and stories, see [[@comics-india|India's favourite comics]].

The Japanese director Akira Kurosawa said that not to have seen Ray's films was like never having seen the Sun or the Moon. [[@hollywood|Hollywood]] directors, including Martin Scorsese, have named him as an influence.

Not everyone agreed. Some Indian critics found his films slow. In 1980, the actor and politician Nargis Dutt complained that Ray's films showed India's poverty to foreign audiences. Ray's admirers answered that his films showed ordinary people with dignity, and that honesty was not an insult.

In 1992 the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences gave Ray an honorary Oscar for his life's work. He was too ill to travel, so the award was filmed at his bedside in Kolkata. The same year, India gave him the Bharat Ratna, its highest civilian honour. He died on 23 April 1992, and his films are still restored and shown around the world.

ज़्यादातर डॉक्टर इसे बस आइसक्रीम वाला सिरदर्द कहते हैं। यह सबसे आम सिरदर्दों में से एक है। सर्वे बताते हैं कि लगभग एक-तिहाई लोगों को यह होता है, और बच्चों को बड़ों से ज़्यादा होता लगता है।

2012 में अमेरिका के शोधकर्ताओं की एक टीम ने 13 बड़ों से कहा कि वे स्ट्रॉ को तालू से सटाकर बर्फ़ जैसा ठंडा पानी चुस्की लेकर पिएँ। टीम ने सिर में खून का बहाव नापा। जैसे ही ब्रेन फ़्रीज़ हुआ, दिमाग के अगले हिस्से के पास की एक बड़ी [[artery|धमनी]] चौड़ी हो गई और खून का बहाव बढ़ गया। जब वह फिर सिकुड़ी, दर्द चला गया।

यह बढ़िया सुराग है। पर 13 लोग छोटा समूह है, और यह अध्ययन बड़े पैमाने पर दोहराया नहीं गया, इसलिए वैज्ञानिक अब भी सावधान हैं कि इससे क्या साबित होता है।

सबसे तेज़ इलाज है तालू को गर्म करना। जीभ को चपटा करके तालू से सटा दो, या थोड़ा गुनगुना पानी पी लो। ठंडी चीज़ें धीरे-धीरे खाओ और उन्हें जीभ के अगले हिस्से पर पिघलने दो। इससे ब्रेन फ़्रीज़ शुरू ही नहीं होता।

यह बेनुकसान है। पर अगर सिरदर्द बिना किसी ठंडी चीज़ के हो, बहुत देर तक रहे या बार-बार लौटे, तो मम्मी-पापा या डॉक्टर को ज़रूर बताओ।

ठंड ही अकेली चीज़ नहीं है जो गलत जगह दर्द जगाती है। कोहनी की एक खास जगह पर चोट लगे, तो छोटी उँगली झनझना उठती है। इसकी वजह है एक नस, जिस पर लगभग कोई गद्दी नहीं होती।

text: Deja vu is the sudden, strong feeling that you've lived this exact moment before, even though you know you can't have. It usually lasts a few seconds and then fades. The name is French for "already seen". Surveys suggest about two out of three people have felt it at least once.

Nobody knows for sure what causes it. Most scientists think it's a hiccup in how your [[@brain-works|brain]] handles [[@memory|memory]]. A part of the brain shouts "familiar!" while another part knows that's not true. The gap between those two messages is the strange, floaty feeling.

myth: Deja vu means you have seen the future or lived the moment in a past life.
There is no scientific evidence for either. The best explanations involve memory and familiarity. In tests, people feeling deja vu can't predict what comes next any better than chance.

sec.t:
One explanation comes from the psychologist Anne Cleary in the USA. She showed people scenes in a computer game, then later showed them new scenes with the same layout but different objects. A bowling alley might be arranged exactly like an earlier junkyard. People often felt deja vu in those new scenes, without remembering the old one.

Her idea is that your brain notices a pattern it has met before but can't find the original memory. So you get familiarity with no label attached. Walking into a new café that's arranged like your aunt's living room could be enough.

sec.h: A brain checking its own files

sec.t:
Deja vu is most common in teenagers and young adults, and becomes rarer as people get older. Being tired or stressed seems to make it more likely. Studies have also found that people who travel a lot report it more often, perhaps because they meet more new places that echo old ones.

For a small number of people, frequent deja vu can be part of a medical condition called epilepsy, when brain signals briefly misfire. If deja vu happens very often or comes with other odd feelings, it's worth telling a parent or doctor. For almost everyone, though, it is harmless.

One older idea said deja vu happens when information reaches the brain by two routes, one a split second slower than the other. The second copy arrives and feels like a memory of the first. It sounds neat, but there's a problem. People who have been blind since birth also report deja vu, set off by sounds, smells or touch, so it can't depend on signals from the eyes arriving out of step.

Doctors operating on the brains of people with epilepsy have also caused deja vu by gently stimulating parts of the temporal lobes, areas near the ears that deal with memory and familiarity. That helps scientists narrow down where the feeling starts, even if they can't yet explain why.

There's a mirror image called jamais vu, French for "never seen". It's when something completely familiar suddenly seems strange, like your own name or a word you write every day. In 2023 researchers Chris Moulin and Akira O'Connor shared an Ig Nobel Prize, a jokey award for science that makes people laugh and then think, for studying it.

The word "deja vu" itself is a traveller, borrowed from French like ballet and café. English is full of [[@words-borrowed|words borrowed]] from other languages, and once you start spotting them, you'll feel like you've seen them everywhere before.

text: India built a set of digital tools that work together, and made them cheap enough for almost anyone. The first was [[@aadhaar|Aadhaar]], a 12-digit ID number linked to [[@biometrics|fingerprints and iris scans]], which began in 2010. Then came hundreds of millions of new bank accounts. Then very cheap mobile data. And then [[@upi-payments|UPI]], which lets anyone send money from a phone in seconds.

Experts often call the first three the "JAM trinity": Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar and Mobile phones. Because they were built as shared public systems, any bank or app could plug into them. That's a big reason India went from mostly cash to billions of digital payments a month within about a decade.

myth: Everyone in India is online now.

India has hundreds of millions of internet users, but hundreds of millions of people still don't use the internet regularly. Women, older people and people in poorer rural areas are much less likely to be online, a gap often called the digital divide.

sec.t:
Before Aadhaar, many Indians, especially the poor and people who had moved for work, had no official proof of who they were. That made it hard to open a bank account or get a SIM card. In September 2010, the first Aadhaar numbers were given out in Tembhli, a village in Maharashtra's Nandurbar district.

Today more than 130 crore people have one. It lets someone prove who they are with a fingerprint at a ration shop or a bank, without carrying papers.

sec.h: A bank account in every home
Data for the price of a cup of tea
sec.t:
In 2016 a new mobile company, Jio, offered free calls and very cheap data. Other companies had to cut prices too. Within a few years, mobile data in India became among the cheapest in the world. Cheap [[@smartphones|smartphones]], many made in India, spread to small towns and [[@villages-india|villages]].

Suddenly, people who had never owned a computer were watching videos, using maps and joining video calls. Many skipped computers altogether and went straight to phones.

In 2016 the National Payments Corporation of India launched the Unified Payments Interface. It lets people send money using a simple ID, a phone number or a QR code, from any bank to any bank, for free. Shopkeepers only need a printed QR code, [[@nfc-tap|no card machine]].

UPI took off after November 2016, when the government withdrew [[@life-money-world|₹500 and ₹1,000 notes]] and people were short of cash. It grew even faster during the COVID-19 [[pandemic|pandemic]]. By 2025, it handled more than 15 billion payments a month, from paying for chai to buying train tickets.

Not everyone welcomed every part. Critics worried that Aadhaar could be used to track people and that their data might leak. In 2017 the Supreme Court ruled that [[@privacy|privacy]] is a fundamental right, and in 2018 it upheld Aadhaar but limited where it could be demanded. India passed a data protection law in 2023.

There are other problems. Online fraud has grown alongside digital payments. Fingerprint scanners sometimes fail for labourers with worn fingertips, leaving people without rations. And many Indians, especially women and older people in villages, still aren't online. Even so, other countries, from [[@singapore|Singapore]] to France, now let visitors pay with UPI, and several are studying how India built its system.

text: AI chatbots are built on large language models, or LLMs. A language model is a huge [[@neural-networks|neural network]] trained on enormous amounts of text: books, websites, articles and code. During training, it plays one simple game over and over. It sees part of a sentence and tries to guess what comes next.

Each time it guesses wrong, its inner numbers are nudged slightly so that next time it does a little better. After trillions of guesses, it gets good at continuing text in a way that sounds natural. Along the way, it picks up grammar, facts, styles of writing and even some ability to follow instructions, without anyone teaching those things one by one.

st.prompt: A chatbot is asked about a very obscure book it never saw in training. What might it do?

options.t: Make up a confident answer that sounds right but is false

st.reveal: Because a language model is built to produce likely-sounding text, it can invent facts, names or quotes when it doesn't know. Researchers call this hallucination. Newer systems try to admit uncertainty or search for sources, but it is always worth checking important answers.

src: Vaswani A. and others (2017), Attention Is All You Need, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems.
Britannica, Large language model.
Stanford University, Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence, AI Index Report.

d.try: Play the next-word game with a friend or family member. One person says the start of a sentence, like "On a rainy day I like to", and everyone writes down the word they think comes next. Compare answers. You'll find some words are very likely and others are surprising, which is exactly what a language model has to judge.
myth: An AI chatbot looks up its answers in a giant database of facts.

A basic language model doesn't store a list of facts. It produces text one piece at a time, based on patterns it learned during training. That is why it can write smoothly yet still get facts wrong, unless it is connected to a search tool or trusted documents.

sec.t:
Computers work with numbers, not words. So first, text is chopped into tokens: whole words, parts of words or punctuation. "Playground" might be one token, or "play" and "ground". Each token gets a number, and then a long list of numbers that describes how it relates to other tokens.

In that list, words used in similar ways end up close together. "Cat" and "dog" sit near each other. So do "Delhi" and "Mumbai". The model doesn't know what a cat feels like, but it knows "cat" often appears near "purr" and "whiskers".

A model trained only to guess the next word will happily continue any text, including rude or false text. So companies train it further. People write example conversations showing helpful answers. Then human reviewers compare pairs of answers and pick the better one, and the model is trained to prefer answers like those.

This step turns a raw text predictor into something that answers questions, explains ideas and declines harmful requests. ChatGPT, released in November 2022, made this kind of chatbot famous. Many companies and research groups now build their own, including groups in India working on models for Hindi, Tamil, Bengali and other [[@languages-india|Indian languages]].

Language models are good at sounding sure, even when they are wrong. They can invent book titles, quotes or facts. This is called hallucination. They may also repeat unfair ideas found in their training text.

They also don't understand the world the way people do. They have never tasted mango or felt rain. Their knowledge stops at the date their training data was collected, unless they are connected to search. That is why it matters to check important answers with trusted sources, and to think about [[@fake-news|fake news]] online.

Training a large model takes thousands of powerful chips running for weeks in huge [[@data-centres|data centres]], using a lot of electricity and water for cooling. People are debating who should own these systems, how they use writers' and artists' work, and how to keep them safe.

Used well, they can explain a maths problem in five different ways, help a farmer read a government form in their own language or help a programmer find a bug. Used carelessly, they can spread errors quickly. The tool is only as good as the questions people ask and the checks they make.

text: The war of the currents was a fierce contest, in the late 1880s and early 1890s, over what kind of electricity should power the United States. Thomas Edison's companies sold direct current, or DC, which flows steadily in one direction. George Westinghouse's company sold alternating current, or AC, which switches direction back and forth many times a second. Its motors and key ideas came from the inventor Nikola Tesla.

AC won because it could be sent long distances cheaply. Today nearly all the electricity reaching homes worldwide is AC. In India it switches direction 50 times a second, at 230 volts. In the United States it is 60 times a second, at 120 volts.

st.prompt: Why did alternating current (AC) win the war of the currents?

options.t: Its voltage could easily be raised and lowered, so it could travel long distances cheaply
It was completely safe to touch
It made light bulbs glow in different colours

st.reveal: With a device called a transformer, AC can be stepped up to very high voltage for long-distance travel, then stepped down to a safer level for homes. Edison's DC could not be changed so easily, so power stations had to be within a couple of kilometres of their customers.

n.certNote: The main events are well documented. Popular stories often turn it into a personal duel between Edison and Nikola Tesla, but historians point out that the real business battle was between Edison's companies and George Westinghouse, and some famous anecdotes are exaggerated.

The charger is a tiny peace treaty from the war of the currents, turning the AC from the wall into the DC your device needs. Never open a charger.
myth: The war of the currents was a personal fight between Edison and Tesla.

Tesla invented key AC machines, but the big business battle was between Edison's companies and George Westinghouse, who bought Tesla's patents. Tesla worked briefly for Edison and they disagreed, but stories of a lifelong duel are mostly a modern exaggeration.

sec.t:
In 1882, Edison opened the first big city power station in New York, using direct current. It worked well, but it had a serious weakness. DC loses a lot of energy as heat when it travels through wires at low voltage. Edison's customers had to live within about a kilometre or two of a power station, so a city would need one in almost every neighbourhood.

Alternating current had an answer. With a simple device called a transformer, AC can be stepped up to very high voltage, sent many kilometres with little loss, then stepped down again near homes. The problem was that nobody had a good motor to run on AC.

Nikola Tesla was a Serbian-American engineer, born in what is now Croatia. He moved to New York in 1884 and worked briefly for one of Edison's companies, but left after a few months, unhappy with how he was treated and paid.

In 1888 he patented a clever AC motor that used a rotating magnetic field. George Westinghouse, an inventor and businessman from Pittsburgh, bought the rights. Westinghouse now had the whole AC package: generators, transformers and motors.

In 1893, Westinghouse won the contract to light the World's Columbian Exposition in [[@chicago|Chicago]]. Tens of thousands of electric lamps glowed across the fairgrounds, all on AC, and millions of visitors saw them.

Then came [[@niagara-falls|Niagara Falls]]. A giant power plant there, built using Westinghouse and Tesla's AC system, began generating in 1895. In 1896, its electricity travelled about 40 km to the city of Buffalo, New York. Long-distance power had arrived, and the war was largely over.

Direct current never vanished. [[@batteries|Batteries]], phones, laptops, LED lights and [[@solar-panels|solar panels]] all use DC, so every charger turns AC from the wall into DC. Modern electronics can now also convert DC to very high voltages, and over really long distances, high-voltage DC lines lose less energy than AC ones. India has some of the longest, including a line about 1,800 km long linking Chhattisgarh to Tamil Nadu.

Tesla died in a New York hotel room in 1943, with little money. Edison is remembered for the [[@light-bulb|light bulb]] and hundreds of other inventions. Between them, they helped bring [[@electricity-history|electricity into homes]] everywhere.

text: Ellis Island is a small island in New York harbour, close to the [[@statue-liberty|Statue of Liberty]]. From 1892 to 1954 it was the United States' busiest immigration station. Ships from Europe docked in New York, and passengers in third class and steerage, the cheapest part of the ship, were ferried to the island to be checked.

Inspectors examined their health and asked questions. Most people were allowed in within a few hours. About 12 million immigrants passed through. Today a large share of Americans, possibly tens of millions, have at least one ancestor who stepped onto that island.

st.prompt: As immigrants climbed the stairs to the Great Hall, doctors secretly watched them. Why?

options.t: To check who was out of breath or limping, as a quick health test
To count how many people had arrived
To choose who would get the best beds

st.reveal: Doctors watched people climb for signs of illness, such as breathlessness or a limp. Anyone who looked unwell got a chalk letter on their coat, such as E for eyes or H for heart, and was taken for a closer check.

Only about 2% were refused entry, usually because of serious illness or because officials thought they could not support themselves. For most people, the whole visit took a few hours.

sec.t:
The station opened on 1 January 1892. The first person to be registered was Annie Moore, a teenage girl from County Cork in Ireland, who had come with her two younger brothers to join their parents in New York. She was given a ten-dollar gold coin to mark the day.

The original wooden buildings burned down in 1897. The grand brick main building that stands today opened in 1900, with a huge hall where thousands of people waited each day.

Most immigrants came from Europe: Italy, Ireland, Germany, Russia, Poland, Greece and many more. Some were escaping poverty or hunger. Others fled [[persecution|persecution]], including many Jewish families from eastern Europe. Most simply hoped for work and a better life for their children.

The crossing by steamship took around one to two weeks. Steerage passengers slept in crowded bunks below deck, often with everything they owned packed into a single trunk or cloth bundle. Many had relatives already in America who had sent money for the ticket.

The busiest year was 1907, when more than a million immigrants entered the country. On 17 April that year, 11,747 people were processed at Ellis Island in a single day.

In the 1920s, new laws set strict limits on how many people could come from each country. Southern and eastern Europeans got small quotas. People from Asia were almost completely shut out.

That hit Indians too. A 1917 law barred most immigrants from a large "Asiatic Barred Zone" that included India. In 1923 the US Supreme Court ruled in a case brought by Bhagat Singh Thind, an Indian Sikh army veteran, that Indians could not become citizens. These limits eased only in the 1940s and 1960s, which is why most of today's large [[@indian-diaspora|Indian American community]] arrived after 1965.

After 1924, most checks happened abroad, and Ellis Island became quiet. It closed in 1954 and slowly fell into ruin. After a major restoration, it reopened as a museum in 1990.

Visitors can now search ship records for their own ancestors, and stand in the Great Hall where so many new [[@new-york|New Yorkers]] once waited, clutching their papers and wondering what came next.

text: Sarla Thakral is the name most people give. In 1936, at the age of 21, she earned her pilot's licence at the Lahore Flying Club, in what was then British India. She flew a small two-seat biplane, a de Havilland Gipsy Moth, alone, and went on to complete 1,000 hours of flying.

But she wasn't the only early flyer. Urmila Parikh earned a licence in 1932, and some members of the Tata family had flown even earlier. Sarla became the best known, and her story was celebrated with a Google Doodle on her birthday in 2021.
