d.try: Fold three paper planes with different wing shapes, narrow, wide and with the tips bent up. Fly each one five times from the same spot and measure the distance. Write down which flew furthest and straightest. Pilots like Sarla learned how small changes to wings change a flight.
myth: Women in India only started flying planes recently.
Indian women were earning flying licences in the 1930s. Some of them flew before many countries allowed women to vote, and India now has one of the highest shares of women pilots in the world.

sec.t:
Sarla was born in Delhi on 8 August 1914. She married young, at 16, and had a daughter by the time she learned to fly. Her husband, P. D. Sharma, was a pilot himself and came from a family with nine pilots. He was the first Indian to earn an airmail pilot's licence, flying between Karachi and Lahore.

He and his father encouraged Sarla to learn. In the 1930s, a married woman climbing into an open cockpit, in a sari, was a bold sight. People came to the airfield to watch.

The Gipsy Moth was a light biplane, with two sets of wings stacked one above the other, made of wood and fabric. It had an open cockpit, no radio and a top speed of about 160 km/h. Pilots wore goggles and a leather helmet. On cold days the wind cut straight through.

To earn her "A" licence, Sarla flew solo and built up her hours slowly. She dreamed of the next step, a commercial licence that would let her fly passengers for pay.

Flying in the 1930s was risky. There were no weather radar systems and few proper runways, and pilots found their way using maps, rivers, railway lines and their own eyes. Planes could stall in strong winds, and engines failed more often than they do now. Every flight Sarla made needed careful planning and a cool head.

{{story:airplanes-fly}}

Then life turned hard. In 1939, her husband died in a plane crash. That same year, World War II began, and civil flying training in India was suspended. Sarla couldn't continue.

She went back to Lahore and studied art at the Mayo School of Art. After [[@partition|Partition]] in 1947, she moved to Delhi with her two daughters. She remarried, built a career as a painter and designed clothes and jewellery. She died in 2008, at 93.

Urmila Parikh of Bombay is recorded as the first woman of Indian nationality to earn a licence, in 1932. Sylla Petit, from the Tata family, got one in India in 1929, but she held British nationality. Each could be called a "first", depending on the rules you use.

After independence, more women took off. Prem Mathur became one of India's first women commercial pilots in the late 1940s. Durba Banerjee later became the first woman pilot at Indian Airlines, the government's domestic airline.

Today India has one of the highest shares of women pilots in the world. About 15 percent of its licensed pilots are women (2020s), compared with roughly 5 percent worldwide. Some fly giant passenger jets, others fly fighter jets for the Indian Air Force, which began training women fighter pilots in 2016.

And women from India have gone even higher. [[@kalpana-chawla|Kalpana Chawla]] flew to space in 1997, and more Indian women are training for missions to come. Across the world, early pilots like [[@mystery-amelia-earhart|Amelia Earhart]] faced the same doubts Sarla did, and one of them vanished over the Pacific in a mystery still unsolved.

text: The Phoenicians were a seafaring people who lived along a narrow strip of coast at the eastern end of the Mediterranean Sea, in what is now mostly Lebanon. They were never one big [[empire|empire]]. Instead they lived in proud, separate city-states, such as Tyre, Sidon and Byblos, each with its own king.

What made them famous was trade. Their ships carried wood, cloth, glass, metals and dye all over the Mediterranean, and they set up trading towns as far away as Spain and North Africa. Along the way they spread a short, simple [[@alphabet-history|alphabet]] that later became the Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic scripts.

st.prompt: How many letters did the Phoenician alphabet have?
st.reveal: The Phoenicians used just 22 letters, all for consonant sounds. Older writing systems, like Egyptian hieroglyphs and Mesopotamian cuneiform, needed hundreds of signs, so this short list was far easier to learn.

n.certNote: Much of what we know comes from Greek, Roman and Hebrew writers rather than the Phoenicians themselves, since few of their own writings survive. A famous story that they sailed all the way around Africa is told by Herodotus, and historians still argue over whether it happened.

sec.h: Cedar, snails and the colour of kings

sec.t:
Writing in Egypt and Mesopotamia used hundreds of picture-signs and took years to learn. The Phoenicians used a [[script|script]] of just 22 letters, one for each consonant sound. A trader could learn it quickly and write down a deal on the spot.

The [[@ancient-greece|Greeks]] borrowed these letters around 800 BCE and added vowels. The Romans then adapted the Greek letters into the Latin alphabet you use for English. The Phoenician letter "aleph", which began as a picture of an ox's head, slowly turned into our letter A. Turn a capital A upside down and you can still see the horns.

Phoenician ships had a large square [[@boats-sail|sail]] and rows of oars for calm days. Sailors steered by the stars at night, and the Greeks are said to have called the Pole Star the "Phoenician star" for that reason.

They founded trading posts, or [[colony|colonies]], across the Mediterranean. The most famous was [[@carthage|Carthage]], in today's Tunisia, which grew so rich that it fought long wars with Rome. Phoenicians also sailed past the Strait of Gibraltar into the Atlantic and built a port at Cadiz in Spain.

The Greek historian Herodotus told a story about Pharaoh Necho II of Egypt, who ruled around 600 BCE. Necho is said to have sent Phoenician sailors south down the Red Sea with orders to come home through the Mediterranean. They supposedly took three years and returned from the west.

Herodotus did not believe one detail: the sailors said that in the far south, the Sun was on their right as they sailed west. Today we know that is just what you would see south of the [[equator|equator]]. Some historians think this detail makes the story more believable. Others say there is not enough evidence to be sure.

Phoenician craftspeople were famous for more than dye. They made fine glass beads and small glass bottles for perfume, and they carved ivory into delicate panels for furniture. Their metalworkers hammered silver and bronze bowls decorated with scenes of hunting and gods, mixing Egyptian and Mesopotamian styles.

Much of what we know about these crafts comes from objects found far from Phoenicia, in Greek tombs, Assyrian palaces and Spanish towns. That tells [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] how widely Phoenician goods travelled. Their own libraries, probably written on papyrus, have mostly rotted away in the damp coastal air.

The Phoenician cities were conquered in turn by the Assyrians, Babylonians, Persians and finally Alexander the Great, who besieged Tyre in 332 BCE. Their language slowly faded. Their letters lived on, carried by the people who had borrowed them.

text: Ranthambore is a tiger reserve and national park in eastern Rajasthan, about 160 km from [[@jaipur|Jaipur]], where two ancient hill ranges, the Aravallis and the Vindhyas, meet. It is dry, rocky forest, dotted with lakes and crossed by old stone walls.

It's one of the best places in the world to see a wild tiger, because its tigers are used to safari jeeps and often walk about in daylight. Rising out of the forest is Ranthambore Fort, a huge hilltop [[fortress|fortress]] first built over a thousand years ago. Today the fort and the forest share the same land: temples and gateways above, tigers, leopards and crocodiles below.

st.reveal: Many families send the first invitation of a wedding to the Trinetra Ganesh temple inside the fort, asking for blessings. Postmen deliver cards addressed simply to Ganesh at Ranthambore.

myth: Tigers only hunt at night.

Tigers are often active at dusk, dawn and night, but they will hunt whenever they get a chance. In Ranthambore, where they are well protected, tigers have often been seen hunting deer by the lakes in broad daylight.

sec.t:
The fort sits on a rocky hill about 200 m above the plains. Its walls run for several kilometres and enclose palaces, step-wells, temples and water tanks. It is believed to have been started in the 10th century by Chauhan Rajput rulers.

Its most famous moment came in 1301, when Sultan Alauddin Khalji of Delhi besieged it. The ruler, Hammir Dev Chauhan, held out for months before the fort fell. His story is still told in Rajasthani ballads.

In 2013, the fort became part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, along with five other [[@rajasthan-forts|hill forts of Rajasthan]]. Inside, the Trinetra Ganesh temple receives wedding invitations from across India, sent by families hoping for the god's blessing.

sec.h: From hunting ground to safe ground
sec.t:
For centuries, the forest was a private hunting ground of the maharajas of Jaipur. Kings, and later British officials and foreign royals, came to shoot tigers here.

In 1973, India launched Project Tiger to save its fast-shrinking tiger population, and Ranthambore became one of the first tiger reserves. It was made a [[@national-parks|national park]] in 1980. Several villages inside it were moved out, with the government offering land and money elsewhere, though some families felt they lost a great deal.

Under protection, the forest recovered. Much of the credit goes to forest officers such as Fateh Singh Rathore, who led the reserve for years, chased off poachers and was once badly beaten by angry villagers. Grass grew back where cattle had grazed it bare, and deer numbers rose. Tigers that had once hidden by day began to roam openly, and wildlife photographers started to arrive from around the world.

{{story:tiger-stripes}}

Ranthambore's most famous tiger was a tigress called Machli, which means "fish" in Hindi, after a fish-shaped marking on her face. She ruled the area around the park's lakes for years and raised several litters of cubs.

In 2003, she was filmed fighting a mugger crocodile about 4 m long, and she won. Machli became one of the most photographed tigers on Earth. She died in 2016, aged about 19, a very old age for a wild tiger. Many of today's Ranthambore tigers are her [[descendant|descendants]].

Ranthambore's success brought a new problem. Young tigers need [[territory|territory]] of their own, and the reserve's limited [[habitat|habitat]] began to fill up. Some wandered into farmland and villages. By 2005, poachers had wiped out every tiger in Sariska, another Rajasthan reserve. From 2008, wildlife officials began moving Ranthambore tigers there, and later to other reserves.

Recent counts put Ranthambore's tigers at roughly 75 to 90, including cubs. India as a whole had about 3,700 wild tigers in its 2022 count, around three-quarters of all the world's wild tigers, from Ranthambore's dry hills to the mangroves of the [[@sundarbans-tigers|Sundarbans]].

Leopards, sloth bears, sambar and spotted deer, wild boar and hundreds of kinds of birds live in Ranthambore too. Most visitors come for one animal, though, and many leave with a story of a tiger strolling past a crumbling stone gate.

text: Enid Blyton was an English writer who wrote more than 600 books for children between the 1920s and 1960s. Her series, such as the Famous Five, the Secret Seven, Malory Towers and The Faraway Tree, have sold hundreds of millions of copies worldwide.

In India, her books became a childhood habit for generations, especially in English-medium schools. They were easy to read, exciting, and came in long series, so a child who liked one had dozens more to find. School [[@libraries|libraries]], lending libraries and second-hand bookshops kept them in circulation for decades. Many Indian adults say Blyton was the first author they read on their own.

sec.h: Picnics, secret passages and no grown-ups
sec.t:
Blyton's stories are built around a simple, irresistible idea: children having adventures without adults. The Famous Five appeared in 21 books between 1942 and 1963. Three siblings, their cousin George and her dog Timmy explore islands, caves and smugglers' tunnels and catch criminals while the adults are elsewhere. Her books have been translated so often that UNESCO's Index Translationum lists her among the most translated authors in the world.

Her boarding-school stories, Malory Towers and St Clare's, follow girls through midnight feasts, lacrosse matches and quarrels. Her [[@fantasy-books|fantasy books]], like *The Magic Faraway Tree*, take readers up a tree to strange lands that drift past at the top.

She wrote in plain words and short chapters, with lots of dialogue. Each chapter ended with a reason to read the next. That made her books ideal for children just starting to read longer stories, much as Harry Potter did later.

{{story:soft-drinks}}

Blyton's books came to India while it was still under British rule, through missionary schools and English-medium education. After independence in 1947, English remained a language of schools and jobs, and her books stayed on library shelves.

They were also cheap and plentiful. Paperbacks were passed between cousins, swapped in school and rented from small lending libraries in many Indian towns. Indian readers learned about scones, ginger beer, potted meat and tinned peaches long before most had tasted them.

Many Indian children also attended schools with houses, prefects and uniforms. The boarding-school world of Malory Towers felt both foreign and familiar.

Blyton has been criticised for a long time. In the 1930s to 1950s, the BBC turned down her work for radio, saying it lacked literary value. Later, some libraries removed her books.

Critics pointed to a limited vocabulary and to attitudes that look badly outdated. Some books contain racist stereotypes. Girls are often shown doing the cooking while boys lead, though George, in the Famous Five, insists on being treated like a boy. Many newer editions have been edited to remove offensive words and update names. In 2022, when English Heritage put up a blue plaque at her former London home, it noted these criticisms.

Supporters reply that her books have got millions of children reading for pleasure, which is no small thing.

Blyton's books are still sold in India, and new editions keep appearing. Many [[@indian-english-writers|Indian writers in English]], and many readers who later moved on to Ruskin Bond, [[@tolkien|Tolkien]] or [[@harry-potter-effect|Harry Potter]], started with her.

Children now also read Indian adventure stories set in places they know. But in many Indian homes, a battered Famous Five paperback is still passed down from parent to child. As an [[@english-spread|English-language]] book loved in a country far from England, it is a small piece of history in its own right.

text: A haiku is a very short poem from Japan. In Japanese, it has 17 sound units arranged in three parts of 5, 7 and 5. It usually captures one small moment in nature, like a frog, a falling leaf or the first snow.

A traditional haiku has a season word, called a kigo, which tells you the time of year. It also has a "cut", a pause that sets two images side by side and lets the reader feel the connection. A good haiku doesn't explain itself. It shows you something and stops.

st.prompt: In English, "Tokyo" has two syllables. How many sound units does it have when counted for a Japanese haiku?
st.reveal: Japanese counts sounds called "on", which are shorter than English syllables. Tōkyō splits into to-o-kyo-o, four units, because the long vowels count twice. That is why a 17-syllable English haiku usually says much more than a Japanese one.

myth: A haiku is any poem with exactly 5, 7 and 5 syllables in English.

The 5–7–5 count comes from Japanese sound units, which are shorter than English syllables. Many haiku poets writing in English use fewer syllables, and care more about a season, a sharp image and a moment of surprise.

sec.h: The frog in the old pond
sec.t:
The most famous haiku was written in 1686 by Matsuo Bashō. In Japanese it reads: *furu ike ya / kawazu tobikomu / mizu no oto*. In English that is roughly: "An old pond. A frog jumps in. The sound of water."

The word *ya* is the cut. First comes the old, still pond. Then, suddenly, a frog and a splash. Then silence again. The frog is the season word, because in Japanese poetry frogs belong to spring. Readers have argued for centuries about what it means: stillness and movement, old and new, or simply a splash heard on a quiet day.

Haiku grew out of a group game. In old Japan, poets met to write linked verse, called renga, taking turns to add lines to a long chain. The opening verse, the hokku, had to set the season and the scene. Over time, poets began writing hokku on their own.

Bashō turned them into serious art. He lived simply, wandered across Japan on foot and wrote travel diaries mixed with poems. The most famous, The Narrow Road to the Deep North, describes a journey of about five months in 1689. At Yamadera, a temple high on a mountain, he wrote of the cicadas' cry seeping into the rocks.

Other masters followed, including Buson, who was also a painter, and Issa, who wrote tenderly about snails, flies and sparrows. In the 1890s, the poet Masaoka Shiki gave the form its modern name, haiku.

{{story:japan-culture}}

Japanese poets count "on", sound units that are shorter than English [[syllable|syllables]]. That is why a 17-syllable English haiku says much more than a Japanese one. Many poets writing in English now aim for about 10 to 14 syllables, in three short lines.

Haiku are often written by hand with a brush, and in Japan the [[@calligraphy|calligraphy]] can matter as much as the words. Schoolchildren in [[@japan-culture|Japan]] write haiku, and [[@newspapers|newspapers]] there print readers' haiku every week.

In the early 1900s, haiku spread to Europe and the Americas. In India, writers in Bengali, Hindi, Tamil and other languages have tried it. The short form suits many languages, because nearly every place has seasons, weather and small creatures worth noticing.

Seasons are the heart of a haiku, though which ones depends on where you live. A poet in Mumbai might choose the [[@frogs-monsoon|monsoon frogs]] or the first mangoes. A poet in Minnesota might choose the first snowfall. The tilt of the Earth that causes [[@seasons-why|seasons]] gives every haiku its clock.

In 2013, NASA invited people to send haiku to Mars. More than 12,000 were submitted, and over 1,100 of them, including the most popular, were put on a disc aboard the MAVEN spacecraft, which went into [[orbit|orbit]] around Mars in 2014. Those 17 sound units travelled further than Bashō ever walked.

text: Yes. In dozens of places around the world, people can turn an ordinary spoken language into [[@whistles|whistles]] and hold real conversations with them. These are called whistled languages.

They are not separate languages. They are a way of whistling an existing one, such as Spanish, Turkish or Greek. The whistler copies the rise and fall of the voice and the way sounds change from vowel to consonant. A trained listener can follow it word by word.

Whistled speech usually grows up where people live far apart in steep mountains or thick forests. A whistle carries much farther than a shout, often several kilometres in good conditions, so a farmer can ask a neighbour across the valley if the goats have wandered over.

st.reveal: A sharp whistle is a narrow, high-pitched sound that stands out against wind and rushing water and travels a long way. In steep valleys or dense forests, where walking over to talk could take an hour, whistling lets people chat across the distance.

sec.t:
La Gomera, one of Spain's Canary Islands off the coast of Africa, is cut by deep ravines. Walking from one side of a valley to the other can take a long time. For centuries, islanders whistled messages across instead, using a whistled form of Spanish called Silbo Gomero.

By the late 20th century, with roads and phones arriving, fewer young people were learning it. In 1999, the island made Silbo a school subject. In 2009, UNESCO added it to its list of the world's Intangible Cultural Heritage, which honours living traditions rather than buildings.

Silbo whistlers often put a finger or two in the mouth to make the sound louder and cup a hand to aim it.

{{story:sound-travel}}

sec.h: How a whistle can carry words
sec.t:
When you speak, your voice makes a mix of many pitches at once. A whistle is much purer, one main pitch that can slide up and down. That narrow, high sound cuts through wind and the noise of rivers and [[@sound-travel|travels a long way]] before it fades.

Some languages, such as the Mazatec language of Mexico or Hmong in Southeast Asia, are tonal: the pitch of a word changes its meaning. Whistlers of those languages mainly whistle the tones. In non-tonal languages like Spanish and Turkish, whistlers turn vowels into different pitches and show consonants as quick jumps, dips or breaks in the whistle.

A whistled sentence is harder to understand than a spoken one, but experienced listeners can recognise a surprising amount.

In the mountains near Turkey's Black Sea coast lies Kuşköy, whose name means "bird village". Villagers there whistle Turkish to talk across the steep hazelnut slopes. UNESCO listed it in 2017 as a tradition in urgent need of protection, because mobile phones have made it less necessary.

Scientists tested whistlers from the area. Spoken language is handled mostly by the left half of the [[@brain-works|brain]]. But when people listened to whistled Turkish, both halves did a fairer share of the work. Whistles, it seems, are processed a bit like music and melody.

In the hills of [[@meghalaya|Meghalaya]], the Khasi village of Kongthong is famous for a related tradition. Each child is given a unique tune by their mother, which works as a name. People call each other across the forest by whistling or humming these tunes.

It is not a full whistled language, since it is used for names and calls, not whole sentences. But it shows the same idea: in hills where shouting fades, a tune can carry a message to exactly the right person.

text: Nobody knows who made the very first potato chip. Thin slices of potato fried in fat appear in an English cookbook from 1817, called *The Cook's Oracle*. An American cookbook printed a similar recipe in 1824.

But the story most people tell is more fun. It says that in 1853, at a lakeside hotel in Saratoga Springs, New York, a diner kept sending back his fried potatoes for being too thick. The cook, George Crum, lost his temper. He sliced them paper-thin, fried them hard and salted them heavily. The customer loved them. It's a good tale, but historians have found no proof it happened.

sec.t:
Saratoga Springs was a fashionable holiday town, full of rich visitors drinking its spring water. George Crum was a real chef there, of African American and Native American heritage, and later ran his own popular restaurant.

What we do know is that thin fried potatoes became a local speciality called "Saratoga chips". They were served in hotels and sold in paper cones. The legend about Crum and the fussy diner seems to have been written down much later, in the 20th century. Some versions even claimed the diner was a famous millionaire, which makes historians more suspicious, not less.

A raw potato is about four-fifths water. When you drop a thin slice into hot oil, that water boils off fast as steam. You can hear it as a fierce sizzle.

Once most of the water is gone, the [[starch|starch]] inside hardens into a light, brittle sheet. Sugars and [[protein|proteins]] on the surface react with the heat and turn golden brown, which gives chips their toasty flavour. This browning shows up all over [[@cooking-science|cooking science]], from toast to roasted coffee.

Thickness is everything. A thick slice stays soft in the middle, like a French fry. A slice a millimetre or two thin dries out right through.

{{story:potatoes}}

sec.h: From hotel treat to every shop
sec.t:
For decades, chips were made by hand and went soft quickly. Two inventions changed that. Machines that peeled and sliced potatoes made chips cheap. And better bags kept the air out.

In the 1920s, a Californian businesswoman named Laura Scudder had workers iron sheets of waxed paper into sealed bags. Chips stayed crisp for longer. Today, chip bags are filled with nitrogen gas instead of air, which keeps the oil from going stale. So the "air" in your packet is there on purpose, though it also makes a small amount look like more.

Chips depend on [[@potatoes|potatoes]], which were first farmed thousands of years ago in the Andes mountains of [[@peru|Peru]] and Bolivia. People there still grow thousands of varieties, in purple, red and yellow.

Spanish sailors carried potatoes to Europe in the 1500s. Portuguese traders and later the British helped spread them in India. Today India is one of the world's biggest potato growers.

In Britain, these are called crisps, and "chips" means thick fries. In the USA they are chips. In much of India people say wafers or chips, and shops sell flavours like masala, magic masala and tomato.

Kerala makes its own famous version from bananas, sliced thin and fried in coconut oil. And in 2009, a British court decided that Pringles, which are made from a dough of dried potato, still count as potato crisps for tax purposes. Their makers had argued they were too different to count.

Food inventions often seem to start with a legend and a happy mistake. The ice lolly has a story like that too, starring an [[@accident-popsicle|11-year-old boy]] and a freezing night.

sec.t:
लाल मिर्च का ज़्यादातर रंग दो रंजकों से आता है। इनके नाम हैं कैप्सैंथिन और कैप्सोरुबिन, और ये लगभग सिर्फ़ मिर्चों में पाए जाते हैं। ये उसी परिवार के हैं जिससे [[@food-why-carrots-orange|गाजर]] का नारंगी रंग और फ़्लेमिंगो के पंखों का गुलाबी रंग आता है।

ये रंजक इतने गाढ़े हैं कि दुनिया भर में मिर्च पाउडर को खाने के प्राकृतिक रंग की तरह इस्तेमाल किया जाता है। हल्की लाल मिर्चों से बनी पैपरिका सॉसेज, चीज़ और चिप्स को रंग देती है। भारत में कश्मीरी मिर्च पाउडर रोगन जोश को बिना ज़्यादा तीखा किए गहरा लाल रंग देता है।

मिर्च के बिना भारतीय खाने की कल्पना करना मुश्किल है, पर मिर्च यहाँ नई मेहमान है। [[@chillies|मिर्च]] अमेरिकी महाद्वीपों से आई है, जहाँ मेक्सिको के लोग कम से कम 6,000 साल पहले से इसे उगाते थे। 1500 के दशक में पुर्तगाली जहाज़ इसे गोवा ले आए। उससे पहले भारतीय रसोइए तीखेपन के लिए काली मिर्च, अदरक और पिप्पली डालते थे।

मिर्च तेज़ी से फैली। वह आसानी से उग जाती थी, अच्छे से सूख जाती थी और काली मिर्च से सस्ती थी। आज भारत किसी भी और देश से ज़्यादा सूखी मिर्च उगाता है। 2022 में दुनिया की कुल फ़सल का एक-तिहाई से ज़्यादा भारत में हुआ। आंध्र प्रदेश का गुंटूर दुनिया की सबसे बड़ी मिर्च मंडियों में से एक है। सीज़न के दिनों में लाल बोरियों से लदे ट्रकों की कतारें मंडी के बाहर लगी रहती हैं, और हवा में इतनी मिर्च घुली होती है कि आने वालों को छींकें आने लगती हैं। भारतीय अपनी उगाई मिर्च का बड़ा हिस्सा खुद ही खा जाते हैं, इसलिए ज़्यादातर फ़सल देश से बाहर जाती ही नहीं।

sec.h: रंग के लिए चुनी गई मिर्चें
sec.t:
कुछ मिर्चें मुख्य रूप से अपने रंग के लिए उगाई जाती हैं। कर्नाटक की ब्याडगी मिर्च झुर्रीदार, गहरी लाल और काफ़ी हल्की होती है। कारख़ाने इसका लाल तेल निकालते हैं, जिसे ओलियोरेज़िन कहते हैं। यह खाने के साथ-साथ लिपस्टिक और नेल पॉलिश में भी डाला जाता है।

किसान लाल मिर्चों को धूप में सुखाने के लिए छतों और खेतों में बिछा देते हैं। फ़सल के मौसम में ऊपर से देखो, तो आंध्र प्रदेश और कर्नाटक के कुछ इलाकों में पूरे के पूरे गाँव सुर्ख़ लाल दिखते हैं। पर धूप रंग को धीरे-धीरे फीका भी कर देती है, इसलिए सबसे अच्छी मिर्चें जल्दी सुखाकर अँधेरे में रखी जाती हैं।

बहुत-से फल पकने पर रंग बदलते हैं, आम से लेकर टमाटर तक। ठंडे देशों में [[@seasons-why|पतझड़]] के मौसम में पत्तियाँ भी कुछ ऐसा ही करती हैं। उनका क्लोरोफ़िल फीका पड़ता है और छिपे हुए पीले और लाल रंजक झलकने लगते हैं। मिर्च की ख़ास तरकीब है उसका तीखा स्वाद, जो गलत जीवों को दूर रखता है, जबकि उसका रंग सही जीवों को बुलावा भेजता है।

text: A roti puffs because of steam. Roti dough is mostly wheat flour and water. When the rolled disc is cooked on a hot tawa, both faces set into thin, tough skins. Then it meets a direct flame, and the water trapped between the skins suddenly turns to steam.

Steam takes up well over a thousand times more room than the water it came from. The skins can't let it out fast enough, so the roti swells into a ball. Wheat's stretchy [[gluten|gluten]] holds it together. Press it and the steam puffs out with a soft hiss.

st.prompt: What fills a roti when it puffs up into a ball?

options.t: Steam from water in the dough

st.reveal: Roti dough has no yeast. When it hits a hot flame, water inside turns to steam and expands hugely. The cooked outer skins are sealed, so the steam has nowhere to go but out, and the roti balloons.

d.try: Watch an adult make rotis. Notice whether the ones rolled evenly, with no thin spots or tears, puff better than the patchy ones. Keep a score for one meal and see if you can guess which roti will puff before it touches the flame.
myth: A roti puffs because air gets trapped in it while the dough is kneaded.
Kneading adds very little air. The puff is steam, made in seconds when water in the dough meets intense heat. Kneading helps by building stretchy gluten that holds the steam in.

sec.t:
Roti, also called chapati, is an unleavened bread. That means it has no [[yeast|yeast]] or [[@baking|baking]] soda to make gas. All its lift comes from water and heat, which is why it can be made in minutes.

The word chapati is often linked to the Hindi word *chapat*, a slap, from the way dough was once flattened between the palms. The puffed version is called phulka, from *phoolna*, to swell. Roti is eaten across north and central India, and in many homes it is still made fresh for every meal.

Indian workers who went abroad in the 1800s and 1900s took roti with them. Many were indentured labourers, workers bound to a contract, sent to sugar estates in the Caribbean, Fiji and East Africa. In Trinidad and Tobago, "roti" now often means a flatbread wrapped around curry and sold as [[@street-food|street food]]. In Kenya and Uganda, chapati is an everyday food.

In the USA, rotis are [[@frozen-food|sold frozen]] in Indian grocery stores from New Jersey to California. There are even countertop machines that knead, roll and cook a roti on their own.

At the Golden Temple in Amritsar, the community kitchen, called a langar, serves free meals to everyone who comes, whatever their religion. On busy days it feeds many tens of thousands of people. Volunteers roll rotis by hand and machines help to keep up.

The langar tradition began with Guru Nanak, the first Sikh Guru, more than 500 years ago, as a way to show that everyone sits as equals. A plate of dal and hot rotis, eaten sitting side by side on the floor, is still at the centre of it.

A fresh roti is soft, but leave it out for an hour and it turns leathery. As it cools, its [[starch|starch]] slowly hardens and the leftover water escapes. Wrapping rotis in a cloth or keeping them in a closed casserole traps the steam and keeps them soft until the [[@thali|thali]] reaches the table.
